name: corpus
description: Cross-video questions over the 30-talk `dataset` index (AI Engineer World's Fair workshops and the UC Berkeley Agentic AI MOOC, 36.6 hours). Hand-written questions; ground truth derived from the index's transcript and on-screen text by `python -m eval.datasets.corpus build` plus curated facts. See eval/datasets/corpus.py for the field semantics.

questions.question: Find all videos that mention Anthropic.
questions.notes: Spoken mentions define the expected set; four more talks only show the word on a slide or model id and are acceptable.

questions.notes: Daniel Han's ASR renders it 'DC R1' once but also says DeepSeek elsewhere.

questions.notes: Sida Wang says 'see the cursor?' about the mouse pointer (excluded: claiming it is wrong). The Vibe Coding workshop's 'but, like the cursor' is ambiguous.

questions.question: Which video discusses Kubernetes, and in what context does the speaker bring it up?
facts: Only Yangqing Jia's 'Evolution of System Designs' lecture discusses Kubernetes.

He brings it up as one of the choices for managing a GPU/compute cluster, as an alternative to a hand-managed cluster run by system administrators (with an aside that Oriol Vinyals was once one of those sysadmins).

questions.question: Which videos mention Notion, the company or its product?
questions.notes: Three talks use 'notion' as an ordinary noun ('the notion that...'); claiming them is wrong.

questions.question: Which talks mention StarCraft?
Which videos mention Hugging Face?
Which speakers mention Kaggle?
In which videos is GRPO (the RL algorithm) mentioned?
Show me the moments where speakers talk about improving RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): better or multimodal retrieval, or evaluating retrieval quality.
facts: Suman Debnath (AWS, VoiceVision RAG) describes multimodal RAG over documents using image/page embeddings with late-interaction (ColPali-style) token embeddings stored in a vector database.
Apoorva Joshi (MongoDB) covers multimodal RAG: embedding page screenshots with a multimodal embedding model into a vector store, and the difficulty of chunking mixed-modality documents.
Sarah Sachs (Notion) explains evaluating retrieval separately from generation, with its own evaluation framework.
Taylor Jordan Smith's evals workshop discusses setting up evaluation for a RAG system.
questions.notes: Other talks mention RAG in passing (RAG poisoning in Dawn Song's lecture, 'RAG is falling out of favor' in Yangqing Jia's) and are acceptable but not required.

questions.question: Which talks explain reward models or reward functions in RL post-training, and what do they say about them?
facts: Jiantao Jiao distinguishes generic preference reward models from task-completion (verifiable) rewards used to post-train agents.
Daniel Han explains that GRPO removes the value model and the reward model, replacing them with reward functions.
Yann Dubois contrasts rule-based (verifiable) rewards with reward models trained to predict human preferences, including LLM-as-a-judge rewards, in RLHF.
Weizhu Chen contrasts RL with a verifiable signal against RLHF, where training a reward model is hard.

questions.question: Where in the library is Mixture of Experts (MoE) explained, and how does each speaker describe it?
facts: Daniel Kim and Daria Soboleva (Cerebras) explain MoE as the architecture their 'mixture of agents' pattern imitates, with agents replacing experts.
Ishan Anand describes MoE as one of the biggest architectural changes since GPT-2, in answer to an audience question.
Yann Dubois names transformers with mixture of experts as the dominant open-source architecture.
Yangqing Jia presents MoE as sparsely activated models that improve efficiency when dense models plateaued.

questions.question: Which speakers refer to Rich Sutton's 'bitter lesson', and how do they use it?
facts: Yann Dubois recommends reading Sutton's blog post and summarises it as: general methods that scale with compute win, which has driven the field.
Peter Stone cites it as the warning that injecting human input can lower ultimate performance, then argues humans and RL can be combined (TAMER + RL).
Oriol Vinyals relates it to whether to bootstrap StarCraft agents with imitation learning from human games before reinforcement learning.

questions.question: Which talks discuss vector databases or vector stores?
Which talks cover guardrails for AI agents, and what kinds of guardrails do they describe?
facts: Dawn Song lists runtime protections: input guardrails, output guardrails, information-flow control and taint tracking, monitoring, and human-in-the-loop; she shows Anthropic's constitutional classifiers as an input-guardrail example.
Clay Bavor says deployed agents must be checked for adherence to policies and guardrails, combining AI checks with deterministic guardrails.
The Vibe Coding at Scale workshop frames custom instructions and custom tools as guardrails that keep AI coding assistants consistent with enterprise conventions.
questions.notes: Four other talks say the word once in passing (Damien Murphy, Taylor Jordan Smith, Thor Schaeff, Mark Backman) and are acceptable.

questions.question: Which talks discuss scaling laws?
facts: Yann Dubois explains scaling laws as tuning at small scale and extrapolating to a large final run, and mentions the Chinchilla paper.
Sida Wang uses scaling laws (consistent gains when model size doubles) as a source of signal for judging benchmark noise.

questions.question: Which speakers mention self-driving cars or autonomous vehicles, and in what connection?
facts: Aman Khan (Arize) started his career on self-driving cars at Cruise, became a PM for evaluation systems there, and applies those lessons to AI evals (he also polls the room about Waymo).
Peter Stone calls an autonomous car an agent that must sense, decide and act, and mentions his DARPA Urban Challenge car.

questions.question: Compare how Noam Brown and Oriol Vinyals talk about self-play: what did it achieve, and where does it break down?
facts: Noam Brown: self-play is behind the game breakthroughs (AlphaGo, Dota, StarCraft, poker) and has not yet appeared in LLMs.
Noam Brown: intuitions about self-play are overfit to two-player zero-sum perfect-information games like Go and chess; the nice properties break outside them.
Oriol Vinyals: naive self-play oscillates (the rock-paper-scissors example), so AlphaStar used a league with exploiter agents.
Oriol Vinyals: AlphaStar was also evaluated by playing humans, not only by climbing self-play Elo.

questions.question: How many talks in the library come from the UC Berkeley Agentic AI MOOC (CS294-196), and who are the speakers?
facts: There are eleven MOOC lectures in the library.
The speakers are Dawn Song, Noam Brown, Yangqing Jia, Jiantao Jiao, Clay Bavor, Sida Wang, Peter Stone, Weizhu Chen, Yann Dubois, Oriol Vinyals and James Zou.
questions.notes: A metadata question: both systems see the video titles (VideoIndex in the agent's system prompt, Gemini in the catalog attached to the request).

questions.question: Which talks are given by Microsoft speakers, and which Microsoft products do they demonstrate?
facts: Jon Peck and Christopher Harrison (Microsoft) demonstrate GitHub Copilot (agent mode / coding agent) in the software development workflow.
Cedric Vidal (Microsoft) demonstrates building code-first agents with Azure AI Agent Service (Azure AI Foundry).

questions.question: Which videos mention Sam Altman?
questions.notes: Nobody says the name; it appears once on a slide in Dawn Song's lecture (acceptable). A good answer says no talk mentions him, or at most points at that slide.

questions.question: Which videos talk about using an LLM as a judge for evaluation?

Summarize the top themes across both event series in the library (the AI Engineer workshops and the UC Berkeley Agentic AI MOOC lectures). What do the two series have in common, and how do they differ?
facts: Both series centre on LLM agents: building them, tool use, multi-agent systems and protocols such as MCP/A2A.
Both series treat evaluation of LLM systems and agents as a major theme (evals tooling and frameworks at AI Engineer; benchmarks and verifiable rewards at Berkeley).
Both series cover RL, post-training and fine-tuning (Daniel Han's and Ilan Bigio's workshops; the Dubois, Jiao and Chen lectures).
AI Engineer is hands-on and applied: workshops on voice AI, RAG and multimodal retrieval, coding assistants, LLM serving/inference, image generation with ComfyUI, and even raising venture capital.
The Berkeley MOOC is lecture-style and more research-oriented: multi-agent and game AI (self-play), agent safety and security, benchmark noise, agents for science, system design.
questions.notes: Whole-library synthesis; scored on the facts only. Both systems see the titles and channels of all 30 videos.

questions.question: Which of these AI topics is talked about the most across the whole library: agents, evaluation, RAG, fine-tuning/RL, or MCP? Rank them and say roughly how concentrated each one is.
facts: Agents is by far the most-discussed topic, spoken about in nearly every talk (about 2,500 spoken mentions in 28 of 30 videos).
Evaluation and fine-tuning/RL come next, each in the low hundreds of mentions and each spread over about 22 talks.
MCP is discussed in about a third of the talks, mostly the AI Engineer workshops, and RAG is the least-discussed of the five (around a dozen talks, mostly in passing).
Agent talk is concentrated in the Berkeley MOOC lectures; MCP is mostly an AI Engineer topic.
questions.notes: Ground truth from spoken-mention counts over the ASR transcripts (agents 2,479 in 28 videos; evaluation 721 in 22; fine-tuning/RL 669 in 22; MCP 210 in 11; RAG 66 in 11).

questions.question: Which model family is named most often across all the talks: GPT/ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama, Claude or DeepSeek? Give the ranking.
facts: GPT/ChatGPT is named most often and in the most talks (roughly 180 spoken mentions across 18 videos).
Gemini is second (about 90 mentions in 13 talks).
Llama is third (about 55 mentions in 11 talks); Claude (about 35 in 9) and DeepSeek (about 40 in 7) trail at similar levels, in either order.
questions.notes: Counts from the ASR transcripts; DeepSeek and Claude are within noise of each other so either order is accepted.
